title: Probability
description: Sample spaces, the addition and multiplication rules, conditional probability, Venn and tree diagrams, and counting

notes.heading: Sample Spaces and the Complement
notes.body:
The **sample space** $U$ is the set of all equally likely outcomes; an **event** $A$ is a subset of it. For equally likely outcomes,
$$P(A) = \dfrac{n(A)}{n(U)}$$
Every probability satisfies $0 \le P(A) \le 1$, and over the whole sample space $P(U) = 1$.

The **complement** $A'$ is the event that $A$ does not happen, and
$$P(A') = 1 - P(A)$$

💡 **Worked Example** — One card is drawn from a standard pack. The probability it is a heart is $\dfrac{13}{52} = \dfrac14$, so the probability it is not a heart is $1 - \dfrac14 = \dfrac34$.

📌 "At least one" almost always means $1 - P(\text{none})$. Reaching for the complement turns a long list of cases into a single calculation.

notes.heading: Combined Events and the Addition Rule
notes.body:
For any two events,
$$P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)$$
The subtraction removes the outcomes counted twice, because those in both $A$ and $B$ appear in each term.

If $A$ and $B$ are **mutually exclusive**, they cannot occur together, so $P(A \cap B) = 0$ and the rule simplifies to $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)$.

💡 **Worked Example** — $P(A) = 0.5$, $P(B) = 0.4$ and $P(A \cap B) = 0.2$. Then
$$P(A \cup B) = 0.5 + 0.4 - 0.2 = 0.7$$

⚠️ **Common mistake** — Adding the probabilities without subtracting the overlap, which can produce a total above 1 — a quick way to spot the error.

📌 Note that "$A$ and $B$" means $A \cap B$ and "$A$ or $B$" means $A \cup B$; read the wording carefully before choosing a rule.

notes.heading: Independent Events
notes.body:
Two events are **independent** when the occurrence of one gives no information about the other. Then
$$P(A \cap B) = P(A)\,P(B)$$
and this equation is also the **test** for independence: if $P(A \cap B)$ equals $P(A)P(B)$, the events are independent; if not, they are not.

💡 **Worked Example** — A fair coin is tossed twice. With $A$ = "first toss is a head" and $B$ = "second toss is a head":
$$P(A \cap B) = 0.5 \times 0.5 = 0.25$$

💡 **Testing** — If $P(A) = 0.4$, $P(B) = 0.5$ and $P(A \cap B) = 0.2$, then $P(A)P(B) = 0.2$, so the events are independent.

⚠️ **Common mistake** — Confusing mutually exclusive with independent. Mutually exclusive events with positive probability are never independent: knowing $A$ happened tells you $B$ did not, which is the strongest possible dependence.

notes.heading: Conditional Probability
notes.body:
The probability of $A$ **given that** $B$ has occurred is
$$P(A \mid B) = \dfrac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}, \qquad P(B) \ne 0$$
Conditioning restricts the sample space to $B$, so every probability is recalculated relative to $B$ alone. Rearranged, the same relationship gives $P(A \cap B) = P(B)\,P(A \mid B)$ — often the quickest route to a joint probability.

💡 **Worked Example** — $P(A \cap B) = 0.2$ and $P(B) = 0.5$, so
$$P(A \mid B) = \dfrac{0.2}{0.5} = 0.4$$

🔑 With independence the conditioning changes nothing: $P(A \mid B) = P(A)$. That is exactly what independence means, and it gives a second test for it.

📌 $P(A \mid B)$ and $P(B \mid A)$ are different numbers in general — the condition and the event cannot be swapped.

notes.heading: Venn Diagrams and Two-way Tables
notes.body:
Both tools organise the same information: they show the four regions $A$ only, $B$ only, both, and neither. The **neither** region is the one students most often forget, and it is usually what the question needs.

**Filling a two-way table** — put the totals on the margins, and remember that each cell is a count of the intersection of its row and column. Convert to probabilities only at the end, by dividing by the grand total.

💡 **Worked Example** — In a class of 30, 18 study maths, 12 study physics and 6 study both.
$$n(M \cup P) = 18 + 12 - 6 = 24 \;\Longrightarrow\; n(\text{neither}) = 6$$
so $P(\text{neither}) = \dfrac{6}{30} = 0.2$.

📌 A question that says "given that" is a conditional probability: take the denominator from the *conditioning* group, not the whole sample space.

illustration.alt: A Venn diagram for two events inside a sample space of sixteen outcomes, showing counts in each region, beside a panel of addition, independence and conditional probability rules.
illustration.caption: The region outside both circles is part of the sample space too, and the conditional probability divides by the conditioning group.

notes.heading: Tree Diagrams
notes.body:
A tree diagram lists the outcomes stage by stage. Along each branch the probabilities multiply; branches leading to the same event are then added.

For **without replacement** problems the denominator of the second stage is one smaller, and the numerators depend on what was taken first.

💡 **Worked Example** — A bag contains 3 red and 2 blue counters. Two are drawn without replacement. Find the probability that both are red.
$$P(RR) = \dfrac{3}{5} \times \dfrac{2}{4} = \dfrac{6}{20} = \dfrac{3}{10}$$

💡 **The "at least one" shape** — With three independent events each having probability $0.1$ of occurring: $P(\text{at least one}) = 1 - P(\text{none}) = 1 - 0.9^3 = 0.271$.

⚠️ **Common mistake** — Treating a without-replacement draw as independent and using the same denominator twice. Check the totals on each branch as you draw the tree.

notes.heading: Counting Techniques
notes.body:
The **multiplication principle**: if one choice can be made in $m$ ways and a second in $n$ ways, the pair can be made in $mn$ ways.

When order matters (arrangements, codes, finishing orders):
$$^nP_r = \dfrac{n!}{(n-r)!}$$
When order does not matter (selections, committees, teams):
$$^nC_r = \binom{n}{r} = \dfrac{n!}{r!\,(n-r)!}$$

The only question to answer first is whether swapping two chosen items produces a different outcome. If yes, it is a permutation; if no, a combination — and the combination is always the smaller number.

💡 **Worked Example** — From 5 people: the number of ways to choose a 2-person committee is $^5C_2 = 10$; the number of ways to appoint a president and a treasurer is $^5P_2 = 20$.

📌 Use the GDC's nCr and nPr commands rather than cancelling factorials by hand — many questions are marked as calculator questions.

questions.stem: The probability that an event $A$ occurs is $0.35$. Find $P(A')$.
A fair six-sided die is rolled once. Find the probability that the score is even.
questions.explanation: The even scores are 2, 4 and 6, so the probability is $\dfrac{3}{6} = \dfrac12$.

questions.stem: What does it mean for two events to be mutually exclusive?
questions.explanation: Mutually exclusive events have no outcomes in common, so $P(A \cap B) = 0$ and they cannot both happen.

questions.stem: Events $A$ and $B$ are independent with $P(A) = 0.5$ and $P(B) = 0.4$. Find $P(A \cap B)$.
In a class of 30 students, 18 study maths, 12 study physics and 6 study both. Find the probability that a randomly chosen student studies neither.
questions.explanation: $n(M \cup P) = 18 + 12 - 6 = 24$, so 6 students study neither, giving $\dfrac{6}{30} = 0.2$.

questions.stem: Events $A$ and $B$ have $P(A) = 0.4$, $P(B) = 0.5$ and $P(A \cap B) = 0.2$. Are the events independent?
choices: no, because the probabilities are different
questions.explanation: $P(A)P(B) = 0.4 \times 0.5 = 0.2$, which equals $P(A \cap B)$, so the events are independent.

questions.stem: A bag contains 3 red and 2 blue counters. Two counters are drawn without replacement. Find the probability that both are red.
questions.explanation: The first draw is red with probability $\dfrac35$; the second is then red with probability $\dfrac24$. Multiplying gives $\dfrac35 \times \dfrac24 = \dfrac{6}{20} = \dfrac{3}{10}$. (Using $\dfrac35 \times \dfrac35$ would be wrong, because the draws are not independent.)

questions.stem: Three independent events each occur with probability $0.1$. Find the probability that at least one of them occurs.
In a group of 100 people, 40 are male, 25 wear glasses and 15 of those wearing glasses are male. Find the probability that a person wears glasses, given that they are male.
questions.explanation: Conditioning on being male restricts the group to 40 people, 15 of whom wear glasses: $\dfrac{15}{40} = 0.375$.

questions.stem: A committee of 3 is chosen from 8 students. How many different committees are possible?
questions.explanation: Order does not matter for a committee, so use combinations: $^8C_3 = \dfrac{8 \times 7 \times 6}{3 \times 2 \times 1} = 56$.

questions.stem: How many 3-letter codes can be formed from 5 different letters if no letter may be repeated?
questions.explanation: Order matters, so use permutations: $^5P_3 = 5 \times 4 \times 3 = 60$. Choosing $^5C_3 = 10$ would count each code only once regardless of order.

questions.stem: Events $A$ and $B$ are independent with $P(A) = 0.6$ and $P(B) = 0.3$. Find $P(A \cup B)$.
